name: night

attributes.attribute: held at the eve of May, brought risk to the cattle
marked as a feast of cattle protection
treated as witches who had shifted shape
spoken over the churns to guard the cream
cattle driven to the rabbit grounds and bled
a ram cut over a standing stone to shed blood
circled at Beltane, the beginning of February, and the start of August

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: May Eve, the opening of Beltane, brought a night when evil could reach the cattle. Farmers feared their herds would sicken and the milk would dry up. Rituals rose to guard that wealth, among them hunting hares as witches in changed form. Herdsmen also spoke charms over the cream churns. In Ulster, cattle were taken to the fairy mounds and bled, with the blood given to the earth. In Devon a ram was bound to a standing stone and cut, so the blood ran over the rock. The cooked flesh was then eaten for good luck. Well sites drew the faithful at Beltane, as at Imbolc in February and Lughnasa in August. The visitor walked the circuit, left a coin or cloth, held silence, and went without turning.

okr.objective: Explain the eve of May as a time of peril for the cattle and the rites against it.
key_results: Beltane eve brought a season when harm could strike the cattle and dry the milk.
At Beltane people sought out hares as witches in changed form and charmed the churns.
In Devon a ram tied to a standing stone was cut and its blood spilled over the rock.
Wells drew pilgrims at Beltane, at Imbolc in February, and at Lughnasa in August.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
